j.learned_fact: Mixing hot water with cold water makes warm water that is "just right"; steam rises from hot water. Also counting to five.
j.thinking_skill: notices that combining two opposites (hot + cold) gives a middle result
j.notes: Pleasant and age-appropriate, but two lessons (temperature mixing and counting bubbles) are stitched together, and "felt shy near the hot water" is an odd word choice for fear/caution.

j.learned_fact: Shaking an instrument fast or slow changes the mood of the music (fast = happy/lively, slow = calm) — a reasonable, if simplified, idea of tempo.
j.thinking_skill: imitates and notices one cause and effect (speed → feeling)
j.notes: The lesson is stated outright by the teacher ("Fast music feels happy... You are learning how speed changes the feeling!") rather than discovered; the odd line "We will serve everyone music today" reads like a bolted-on vocabulary word and will confuse a four-year-old.

j.learned_fact: A star shape has five points, and counting as you draw helps you make two shapes match; six points makes a different shape.
j.thinking_skill: compares two shapes and identifies the variable (number of points) that made them differ
j.notes: Flat, clipped sentences with little warmth or dialogue; Maya is a device rather than a character, and the "lesson" repeats itself in the last paragraph.

j.learned_fact: "An axle" is "like a stick between the wheels" — accurate definition; but the story then falsely shows dried painted circles actually spinning, which is impossible.
j.thinking_skill: notices wet paint smears and waits for it to dry (one cause and effect)
j.notes: The central event is physically impossible — a painted circle cannot turn — so the "discovery" is nonsense, and the closing line ("wheels could row him around the driveway") uses the wrong word. Vocabulary ("axle," "true") is bolted on via teacher exposition.

j.learned_fact: Ovens are very hot and hot things burn skin, so you stay away; oven mitts/gloves are used to take food out.
j.thinking_skill: accepts a stated cause and effect (hot oven burns skin)
j.notes: The toy robot and marker-dotted bananas are a nonsensical inserted episode that goes nowhere; the safety lesson is delivered as a direct parental line rather than through events.

j.learned_fact: Fairness in a game can mean everyone gets the same number of turns/kicks.
j.thinking_skill: recognizes a rule (equal turns) as fair
j.notes: "Anthony did not frown anymore" refers to a frown that never happened, and the fairness lesson is stated flatly by the narrator instead of being felt; there is no real problem or tension.

j.learned_fact: "Half means we cut it down the middle" — half is smaller than a whole; recipes use measured amounts like two cups of flour.
j.thinking_skill: follows a sequence and compares half to a whole
j.notes: Pleasant but slight: no problem to solve, and the "half" concept is below an 8-year-old's level (grade 3 works with thirds, fourths, doubling a recipe). The closing line "You learned something real today" states the lesson instead of showing it.

j.learned_fact: Brazil grows about a third of the world's coffee thanks to warm climate and rich soil (roughly true); the "steep hillsides" emphasis is misleading — much Brazilian coffee grows on plateaus and rolling highlands.
j.thinking_skill: sorts sources by purpose (entertain, persuade, inform)
j.notes: The "advertisement" appears out of nowhere — no ad was among the three sites — and the closing paragraph states the lesson outright instead of letting the map-making show it.

j.learned_fact: "Two parts" in a recipe means the same unit measured twice, so ratios require a consistent measure — accurate; though the chemistry framing ("Make Your Own Molecule") is misleading, since mixing colors isn't making a molecule.
j.thinking_skill: identifies her error by comparing her method to a model's
j.notes: Vocabulary and sentence rhythm sit well below a 10-year-old's level, and the insight (measure instead of guess) is too obvious for that age; the "molecule" label is scientifically inaccurate for color mixing.

j.learned_fact: Ancient cities grew powerful by controlling water sources and trade routes, and declined when those routes shifted or were blocked — accurate but generic, with no named city or example.
j.thinking_skill: transfers an abstract principle by analogy (field control = resource control)
j.notes: The history content is summarized by the narrator rather than dramatized, and stays vague (no actual Roman city named), so it reads as a bolted-on lesson. The first-date romance frame also skews older than 11.

j.learned_fact: The Montgolfier brothers flew the first hot air balloon in 1783, having found that heating air makes it lighter (accurate). But the story's chemistry is vague or wrong: Sophie never learns the actual reaction (acid + bicarbonate → carbon dioxide), and "watching the atoms and molecules rearrange themselves" is impossible to see; "two substances could blow apart when mixed" is garbled.
j.thinking_skill: varies one quantity while holding the other constant and looks for a pattern
j.notes: The claimed insight is empty — Sophie ends "understanding" without any explanation ever being stated, and her final test uses one tablespoon for no stated reason. For a 10–11-year-old the conceptual payoff is too thin and one sentence is factually impossible.

j.learned_fact: Food chains/energy pyramids: plants feed rabbits, rabbits feed hawks, so predators must be far fewer than prey.
j.thinking_skill: notices a second-order consequence (predators starve when prey run out)
j.notes: The ecology concept (simple food chain) is elementary-level for a 12-year-old, and the insight is handed to Raphael by the teacher's question rather than reasoned out; the manager's knowing smiles are a contrived device.

j.learned_fact: A single trial can mislead; repeated trials reveal patterns — e.g., steel samples from one cheap supplier consistently failed at lower stress, and free-throw accuracy correlated with practice the night before.
j.thinking_skill: notices a correlation across repeated trials and considers confounding variables
j.notes: The lesson about sample size is delivered almost entirely through Dr. Chen's explicit speeches, and the story stops at the moral rather than dramatizing it; the stray reference to "the son of the company's owner," never introduced, is a coherence break. Vocabulary and emotional stakes sit below a 9th-grade reader.

j.learned_fact: Brown-eyed parents who are both heterozygous (Bb) can have a blue-eyed (bb) child. However, the story's climactic insight is logically false: a single blue-eyed child already proves both parents are carriers, so a second one adds no certainty; it also presents eye colour as a simple one-gene trait, which is a known oversimplification.
j.thinking_skill: infers hidden genotypes from observed phenotypes (attempted probabilistic reasoning from evidence)
j.notes: The central "aha" is mathematically wrong—one blue-eyed child already establishes both parents as carriers—so the story rewards a false insight. The tacked-on town-council/zoning analogy is vague and the plot is almost entirely a boy filling in a worksheet, with no stakes or characterization for a 14-year-old reader.

j.learned_fact: Latitudes south of the equator are expressed as negative numbers (Sydney ≈ -33.8°), so a conditional that rejects values below a threshold will wrongly exclude southern-hemisphere cities.
j.thinking_skill: isolates a variable by testing the same value in different code paths to localize a bug
j.notes: Low stakes and almost no external conflict; the closing lines state the moral a bit too explicitly ("You had to think about what your data actually meant"). Technical detail stays vague—we never see actual code, so the debugging feels summarized rather than dramatized.

j.learned_fact: Pricing must cover materials plus labour: $8 supplies + 6 hours at ~$7.50/hr ≈ $53, so a $35 price loses money; scarcity and reduced labour time can raise margin.
j.thinking_skill: recalculates cost structure and redesigns the product's inputs to change the margin
j.notes: The clerk functions as an economics tutor rather than a person, and the story does the reasoning in her dialogue; also a typo ("He remember") and the $45 minimum-wage figure is vague/below most real minimums. For 17-year-olds the conceptual load (opportunity cost, break-even, scarcity pricing) is modest and could be pushed further.

j.learned_fact: Off-by-one array errors: a loop indexing 24 positions crashes on a 23-element data set, fixed by checking array length — accurate. The claimed mechanism (urban heat islands drive vertical currents that "concentrate pollutants") is muddled/dubious; rising warm air would generally disperse, not concentrate, CO2, and the story asserts it as settled EPA fact.
j.thinking_skill: traces variable values to isolate a bug, then seeks a causal explanation for an unexpected data pattern
j.notes: The second half turns into narrated exposition plus a tidy moral about debugging as a way of thinking; the central science claim is shaky and stated authoritatively, which undercuts the educational payoff. Marcus is a prop rather than a character, and for a 16-17-year-old reader the emotional stakes and prose complexity are modest.

j.learned_fact: That probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive (overlapping) events cannot simply be added — true as far as it goes, but the story never states the correction (subtracting the intersection), and the invented card problem's numbers (0.5 vs 0.35) are never made checkable, so the "lesson" is unverifiable hand-waving.
j.thinking_skill: diagnoses a conceptual error behind a correct-looking calculation
j.notes: The romantic-nervousness prose is genuinely well observed, but the mathematical core is vapour: the problem is never specified, the fix is never shown, and 0.35 arrives by authorial fiat. "Locked her hand around his wrist" is an oddly violent phrasing for a tender beat.

j.learned_fact: That generative AI tools can produce visual concepts from text prompts, and that this raises questions of attribution in art — true, but stated only in passing.
j.thinking_skill: distinguishes influence from imitation and questions provenance of authorship
j.notes: Competent, quiet interiority, but the final paragraph collapses into a muddled abstraction ("Mankind might increasingly rely on machines...") whose logic doesn't parse; the moral is asserted rather than earned. For a 17-year-old the conceptual stakes stay shallow — no real counterargument to the AI artist is ever weighed.

j.learned_fact: Concentrated garment sourcing (e.g., Bangladesh textiles) makes supply chains fragile: port congestion abroad delays materials, raises costs, triggers contract penalties; diversifying suppliers adds cost and spreads orders thinner. Accurate, if generic.
j.thinking_skill: weighs trade-offs in a system with no optimal solution
j.notes: The insight is delivered mostly through summarized narration and a mother's tidy exposition rather than dramatized events; nothing is at stake for Lily, so the story reads as a framed mini-lesson on supply chains. Prose is capable but under-challenging for a 12th-grade reader in subtlety and subtext.

j.learned_fact: "Perspicacious" means insightful, not sweaty; also quotidian, recalcitrant, ephemeral, sesquipedalian used in context — all accurate.
j.thinking_skill: infers a general principle (words stick through contextual use, not definition) from observed classroom behaviour
j.notes: The premise is a thinly veiled vocabulary lesson, and the long penultimate paragraph is the narrator explicitly articulating the pedagogical thesis — an essay conclusion wearing a story's clothes. Plot is static: nothing is at stake and Isla never acts.
